tone_statements.citation: Davis, Tyler D. 2017. Verb stem alternation in Sizang Chin. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 115 pp.
tone_statements.quote: 2.5 Tones: In Sizang there are three tones viz. i) Level tone ii) Rising tone and iii) Falling tone. These tones are also easily attestable by minimal pairs. The three contrastive tones in a syllable are illustrated in Table 2.3. The level tones left unmarked above the vowel whereas the rising tone is marked as / ́/ above the vowel and the falling tone is marked as / `/, above the vowel. The Level tone maintains an even pitch. ... 1. saŋ ‘school’ sáŋ ‘received’ sàŋ ‘height’ 2. hay ‘mango’ háy ‘cup’ hày ‘late’
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.5 Tones, pp. 75-76 with Table 2.3; also 2.1 p. 26 'There are three tones and one junctures'
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (level, rising, falling) shown by minimal triplets; author says tones were not instrumentally analysed; tone changes with prefix ə- (pá ~ əpa) and in verb stem II (level > rising).

tone_statements.quote: Sizang only has three tones. Mid-Level (33) /aː/, Rising (34) /ǎː/, and Falling (42) /âː/. Stern (1963, pp. 229–230) maintained there was a high-level tone /áː/ as well, so his original transcriptions are unmodified when presented in this thesis, as the environments in which this high tone surfaces are not yet clearly defined. A minimal set of tonal contrasts is given in Table 5. Table 5 Sizang toneme contrasts ... Mid-Level (33) saː ‘hot’ Rising (34) sǎː ‘meat’ Falling (42) sâː ‘think’
tone_statements.locator: p. 7, sec. 1.3 Phonological inventory and transcription, with Table 5
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (mid-level 33, rising 34, falling 42) with a minimal triplet; Stern's fourth high-level tone set aside. Stem II verbs mostly take falling tone (after Button 2011). Nothing on stress.

Stern’s (1963:229-30) observation that in Sizang it often surfaces as a low level tone [tone letter] is also supported here, but his treatment of the frequent Sizang high level tone [tone letter] as part of the basic tone system is identified by Luce (1962:68) as a result of sandhi.

tone.says: First-hand comparative statement: on weight-bearing syllables Mizo and Zahau have four tones, Thado, Zo, Tedim and Sizang three (tone categories I, II, III with a chart of contours per language); TC-I surfaces in Sizang often as low level (agreeing with Stern), and Stern's extra high-level tone is treated, after Luce 1962:68, as a sandhi product rather than a basic tone; TC-III is a falling tone in all six languages and is associated with derived (stem II / nominal) forms; stopped syllables who…

tone.quote: A system of three tones is probably the norm for all languages, as mentioned by Luce (1985). These tones are rising, mid and falling tone. However, some languages add one or two tones. If a language has four tones, the fourth tone tends to be a low tone and if there are five tones, the fifth tone tends to be a high tone.
